scenes.name: sixty-four warps and the turn counter
scenes.visual: A calendar grid of 48 clock cycles for one scheduler. With all 16 of its warps ready, warp zero gets a turn on tick 1, tick 17, tick 33, and tick 48. A clock timeline demonstrates that each thread executes once every 16 ticks, illustrating why individual threads are slow while the aggregate is fast.

beats.say: Sixty-four warps of thirty-two threads fill one multiprocessor to capacity: two thousand and forty-eight resident threads.
beats.show: A multiprocessor card displays 64 warp slots in four columns of 16. A gauge reads 'Occupancy: 100% · 2,048 resident threads'.

beats.say: Every cycle, each of the four schedulers issues one instruction. Spread over sixteen warps, each thread moves once every sixteen ticks.
beats.show: A timeline of ticks scrolls by. Gold cells highlight every sixteenth tick: tick 1, tick 17, tick 33, showing warp zero's turns.

beats.say: At nearly two billion ticks a second, that is about a hundred and twenty-four million instructions a second per thread.
beats.show: A rate readout lands beside the timeline: '1.98 GHz ÷ 16 = ~124 million instructions per second per thread'.

beats.say: Across the entire chip, that adds up to thirty-three point five trillion thread-instructions every second. The speed is in the count, not in any single thread.
beats.show: The counter multiplies across all 132 multiprocessors to '33.5 trillion thread-instructions per second'. Takeaway: 'slow threads are not a bug; they are how 64 warps share 4 schedulers'.

scenes.name: Little's law: what must be on the road
scenes.visual: The pizza delivery analogy of Little's Law, transitioning to HBM. To deliver 3,352 bytes every nanosecond across a 273 nanosecond round trip, 915 kilobytes must be in flight at all times. A bar chart verifies that 2,048 threads per SM provide just enough requests to saturate the memory bus.

beats.say: To keep any delivery pipeline full, you must know how much work has to be on the road.
beats.show: A roadside delivery diagram appears: an oven on the left, customers on the right, and delivery drivers in transit between them.

beats.say: If a pizza leaves every five minutes and a round trip takes thirty minutes, you need six drivers on the road at all times, or the oven sits idle.
beats.show: Six delivery vehicles animate along the route. Formula: 'items in flight = rate × trip time = 12 per hour × 0.5 hours = 6 drivers'.

beats.say: This is Little's law. For high-bandwidth memory delivering three thousand three hundred and fifty-two bytes a nanosecond across a two hundred and seventy nanosecond trip, nine hundred and fifteen thousand bytes must be on the road at every moment.
beats.show: The diagram transforms into the HBM memory bus: '3,352 bytes/ns × 273 ns = 915,096 bytes in flight'. Tag: '≈ 915 KB must be requested and traveling at all times'.

beats.say: Divided across one hundred and thirty-two multiprocessors, each unit must keep about seven thousand bytes in flight.
beats.show: The required load splits: '915,096 bytes ÷ 132 SMs = 6,933 bytes in flight per SM'.

beats.say: If every one of the two thousand and forty-eight threads has one four-byte load outstanding, that is eight thousand bytes: just enough to saturate the bus.
beats.show: A comparison bar appears: '6,933 bytes needed' vs '8,192 bytes from 2,048 threads (1.18×)'. Takeaway: 'full thread occupancy is what provides enough memory requests to reach full bandwidth'.

scenes.name: the complete execution chain
scenes.visual: The complete execution hierarchy assembled into one nesting diagram: from an individual thread lane up to the full H100 GPU package.

beats.say: Here is the complete hierarchy of execution on the chip, from the thread to the package.
beats.show: A nested diagram begins with a single thread lane: 'Thread · one sequence of arithmetic'.

beats.say: Thirty-two threads make a warp, executing one shared instruction in lockstep.
beats.show: The thread nests inside a warp container: 'Warp · 32 threads, 1 instruction'.

beats.say: A block holds up to thirty-two warps, sharing one slice of on-chip scratchpad memory.
beats.show: The warp nests inside a block container: 'Block · up to 32 warps (1,024 threads), 1 shared memory'.

beats.say: A multiprocessor holds up to sixty-four warps across four schedulers, and one hundred and thirty-two multiprocessors make the chip.
beats.show: The block nests inside a multiprocessor tile: 'Multiprocessor · 64 warps (2,048 threads)'. That tile multiplies into the full chip: 'H100 · 132 SMs = 270,336 threads in flight'. Takeaway pill: 'threads make warps, warps make blocks, blocks fill multiprocessors'.

checks.claim: Thread instruction rate: 1.98 GHz / 16 cycles = 123.75 million instructions per second per thread
Chip thread instruction rate: 132 SMs * 128 lanes * 1.98 GHz = 33.454 trillion instructions per second
Little's law bytes in flight: 3,352 GB/s * 273 ns = 915,096 bytes
2,048 threads * 4 bytes = 8,192 bytes, which is 8,192 / 6,932.55 = 1.18x of needed
Execution chain total: 32 threads * 64 warps * 132 SMs = 270,336 threads in flight
